# The Cartographer of Small Things

There is a man in my building who spends his evenings cataloging the sounds he hears through the walls. He keeps a notebook — not a journal, a *notebook*, with ruled lines and a pen clipped to the spine — and he writes things like: "7:14 PM. The faucet in 4B has developed a hesitation between drips. It is learning to stall." Or: "11:02 PM. Someone is watching television with the subtitles on. The text scrolls in silence. I cannot tell if they are deaf or simply impatient."

I don't know how I learned this about him. Maybe he told me once in the elevator, mid-sentence, as though we'd been conversing for years and he had simply picked up where he'd left off. Maybe I read his notebook when he left it on the laundry room table. Either way, I think about him often — not because his hobby is unusual (it isn't, not really; we are all catalogers of one kind or another), but because I envy the precision of his attention.

Here is what I mean:

Last Tuesday, my daughter drew a picture of our house. She is seven. She drew it from above, as though she were floating — a cross-section roof with the rooms laid open beneath it, like a dollhouse. My wife sat on the couch with a glass of wine, her legs crossed, her laptop open but forgotten. I was standing in the kitchen, doing dishes. My daughter rendered all of this with careful, waxy lines: the dishwater, the wine glass, the slight lean of my posture as I scrubbed a plate. She even drew the steam.

I looked at the drawing for a long time and realized I had not *seen* any of that. I had been thinking about an email I hadn't answered. I had been thinking about a dream from the night before in which I was late for something — I can never remember what — and the hallway kept extending ahead of me, room after room, all of them locked.

My daughter had not been thinking about anything. She had been *looking*.

This is what I mean about the cartographer of small things. The man in apartment 3A understands that reality is not a narrative — it is a collection of data points so dense and overlapping that the only honest thing you can do is write them down as they come. The faucet's hesitation. The subtitle's scroll. The particular pitch of a neighbor's sneeze, which tells you what season it is.

I have started to pay more attention myself, though it's difficult. The problem is that my mind is almost always *elsewhere*. I am writing this, for instance, and I'm already thinking about the next sentence, and the sentence after that, and whether this piece will be any good, and what you'll think of me for writing it. I am never exactly where I am. I am drafting, always drafting, always in revision.

But yesterday morning I sat on my back porch with coffee and I forced myself to count things. Not for a purpose. Not for a poem or a story. Just to count.

There were fourteen bird species in the tree across the yard. I'm fairly sure of this — though "fairly sure" is itself an admission of inattention, because true cartography does not deal in *fairly sure*. There were three ants on the railing, all heading in the same direction, and then one ant heading the opposite way, which I decided was either brave or lost. The coffee was warm but not hot — my wife makes it at 5:45 and I drink it at 7:15, and this twenty-minute gap has created a specific temperature that I have come to associate with the act of *sitting still*.

None of this is important. I understand that. I am not trying to make a case for the profundity of ants or the significance of lukewarm coffee. What I am trying to say — and I will admit that the *trying* is the problem — is that there is a kind of life that is lived at the surface of things, where everything is wet with detail, and there is a kind of life that is lived underneath, in the architecture of thought and worry and planning, and that I have spent most of mine underground.

My daughter's drawing hangs on the refrigerator now. She drew the steam rising from the dishwater and I did not know steam could be drawn. You have to shade it, she explained, with the side of the crayon, not the tip. You have to move it gently. You have to not press too hard.

The man in 3A moved out last week. I saw him in the hallway carrying a box of books and that notebook. He nodded at me — a small, cartographer's nod — and I nodded back. I wanted to ask him what he'd heard through the walls. I wanted to ask him everything. But he was already walking, and I was already standing in my doorway, and the distance between *wanting to ask* and *actually asking* is, as always, the longest hallway I've ever walked.

I hope wherever he went, the walls are thin.
